Nigel Farage has accused British Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying Brexit voters by bringing Britain back into parts of the EU single market, as the two sides prepared to seal a series of agreements at a summit in Brussels on Friday.

Speaking to Euronews' Europe Today as Burnham arrived for his first EU summit since taking office in July, the Reform UK leader and longtime Brexit campaigner said he was "pretty angry" at having to fight the Brexit battle all over again.

"What is happening this morning in Brussels is Andy Burnham is bringing us back into the single market in the areas of foodstuffs and farming," Farage said.

He argued that Britain would have to accept EU regulations without having a vote on them, describing the move as a betrayal of Labour's promise not to rejoin the single market.

But Farage struggled to offer a convincing rebuttal to Burnham's argument that Brexit had damaged Britain's economy and international standing.

He claimed Britain's global influence had actually increased since leaving the EU, citing its support for Ukraine and the AUKUS nuclear submarine agreement with Australia.

"There's no question we stand taller," he insisted.

On the economic damage, however, Farage argued that the Covid pandemic made it difficult to assess Brexit's impact. He claimed Britain had prospered in sectors such as artificial intelligence and financial services, while dismissing the EU single market as a "failing, backward model".

Farage was more candid about immigration, acknowledging that Brexit had failed to deliver one of its central promises.

"It was the biggest," he said when asked whether the failure to control immigration was Brexit's greatest disappointment.

He blamed successive Conservative governments for allowing record immigration despite regaining control of Britain's borders.

Farage also acknowledged that many Britons felt Brexit had failed to deliver, but insisted this did not mean they wanted to reverse it.

He warned that reopening the question of EU membership would divide the country and demanded another referendum if Burnham sought to rejoin.

"If Labour, if Burnham, fights the next election on a ticket of rejoining the EU, he'd have to have a referendum," Farage said.

Asked whether Britain could be back in the EU within five years, Cremer replied: "That would be my wish."

HPV vaccination rates vary by country and gender, EU health data shows.

A vaccine against a common virus can prevent several cancers — but whether teenagers get it depends largely on where they live, European health data shows.

Teenage girls in the Nordics, Spain and Portugal are more likely to be vaccinated against HPV, or human papillomavirus, than anywhere else, while boys in Central and Eastern Europe are least likely to get the jab, according to data from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

HPV is a group of common viruses, some of which spread through sex. Most infections clear up on their own, but certain types can linger and cause cancer years later. That includes cervical cancer — which kills about 280,000 women worldwide each year — and rarer cancers in both women and men.

HPV vaccines have been authorised in the European Union since 2006, and most countries recommend that all girls and boys are vaccinated by the time they are 15. Older people who have not been vaccinated can get catch-up jabs.

Health authorities have long recommended two doses, but dozens of countries have switched to a single-dose schedule. Research indicates that even one jab may be enough to protect against infection with the HPV strains most likely to cause cancer.

Countries that adopted the vaccine early on, such as Sweden and Scotland, have reported far lower rates of cervical cancer in the years since. But there are wide gaps in who actually gets the HPV vaccine, ECDC data shows.

In Portugal, 95% of girls get all doses of the HPV vaccine by age 15, compared with just 4% in Bulgaria. The rates are generally lower among boys, who have only been offered HPV vaccination in more recent years. It ranges from 94% of boys in Portugal to 1% in Romania.

On average, 64% of girls and 51% of boys had gotten all doses of the HPV vaccine by age 15, below the European Union’s 90% target for girls.

Several countries have taken steps to boost immunisations. In 2021, Sweden began offering catch-up jabs for women who were not vaccinated when they were younger, as part of its campaign to become the first country to eliminate cervical cancer. By 2025, Sweden also had one of the smallest gender gaps in HPV vaccination: 91% of girls and 87% of boys had gotten the jab by age 15, according to ECDC data.

Meanwhile, France launched a school-based HPV vaccination programme in 2023; in the first year, vaccination rates climbed from 31% to 48% among 12-year-olds. And Bulgaria began offering free HPV vaccination to boys in 2025.

Yet HPV vaccination rates have also fallen in some countries, largely due to social media misinformation around the jab, according to a set of reviews carried out last year by Cochrane, an influential nonprofit research group.

In Romania, Bulgaria and Croatia, rumours that the HPV vaccine could harm children or cause side effects, coupled with a lack of trust in health authorities, help explain why vaccine uptake has remained low, another study in the BMJ Public Health journal found.

There is no evidence that the HPV vaccine causes commonly reported side effects, according to Cochrane, which analysed both clinical trials and real-world studies involving more than 132 million people.

Teenage girls who were vaccinated against HPV were 80% less likely to develop cervical cancer than unvaccinated girls, the Cochrane review found.

The researchers said the HPV vaccine is most effective when people get it before they are exposed to the virus or become sexually active.

Damage from the unrest around France's October cost-of-living protests could cost insurers €207 million. France Assureurs says the estimate is "particularly high for events concentrated into 24 hours". Over 95% of the estimated cost relates to damage to business property.

The total amount of insured damage from unrest and looting around cost-of-living protests in France on 17 and 18 October could reach €207 million across 5,280 claims, according to an initial assessment by France Assureurs, the French insurance industry body, based on data available as of 12 November.

More than 95% of the estimated total cost, or €198mn, relates to damage to business property, across 4,050 claims. Damage to individuals' property could reach €3.5mn across 370 claims, while damage to vehicles could reach €6mn across 860 claims.

France Assureurs president Florence Lustman said, "The cost of the urban violence on 17 and 18 October is particularly high in view of the brevity of the events".

The statement added that the 2005 riots cost insurers €209mn over four weeks, while the 2018-2019 Yellow Vests movement cost €256mn over several months.

Government sets out grants for small businesses

The government published the rules on Friday in the Official Journal (source in French) for grants to eligible businesses with fewer than 50 employees that suffered damage during the urban violence in October and November.

To receive a grant of €1,000 to €10,000, eligible businesses must apply via the Démarche numérique platform "no later than six weeks after the date of signature" of the decree.

The decree says the grants are aimed at the small businesses worst affected by damage during unrest around demonstrations held between 17 October and 19 November 2026, when the decree was signed.

In each region, a committee chaired by the regional prefect or their representative will review applications from local businesses.

The committee will decide on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the scale of the operating losses, the nature and extent of the damage, and eligibility for other national or local support schemes.

Emergency funds have also been released by local authorities in the worst-affected areas, while an interest-free loan from Bpifrance allows affected shopkeepers to borrow up to €50,000, including to replenish stock ahead of Christmas.

The main civil servants’ union has criticized senior management for letting staff learn of the breach from the press, as employees fear their personal data is at risk.

European Commission staff have voiced frustration over the lack of communication surrounding a large-scale cyberattack that struck the institution in October.

Renouveau & Démocratie (R&D), the main trade union representing EU civil servants, criticised the Commission's handling of the incident, saying staff were not notified when the cyberattack was detected on 22 October and that the institution only acknowledged it after it was reported in the media.

“This failure of internal communication is unacceptable,” R&D chair Cristiano Sebastiani said in a statement on Thursday. Staff should not “have to learn from a newspaper headline” that their personal data could be at risk, he added.

For several days, officials have been unable to access Sysper, the internal HR platform where they check salary information, request holidays and sick leave, submit timesheets and sign up for training.

According to R&D, civil servants have been contacting the union to express their concern and anger.

“Discovering this from the press is absurd. Transparency would have been a better choice,” a Commission official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

The Commission eventually notified staff in an internal note on Friday, a day after the news was first reported by the media. “The Commission has recently been targeted by a series of cyberattacks, including through the use of AI,” it reads. The note says the breaches affected a limited number of systems and that there is no evidence of a data breach affecting staff as a whole.

In a further statement to Euronews, Sebastiani described the note as “absolutely inadequate given the gravity of the failure” and called on senior management to issue a formal apology.

Most civil servants have experienced only minor disruption to their daily work, but the incident has raised concerns. “The mere possibility of my data being leaked scares me, particularly given all the phishing emails I get every day,” another official told Euronews.

A Commission spokesperson said on Thursday that the attack relied on a publicly available AI tool, without saying whether it was still ongoing or attributing it to a specific actor. The tool, called ARTEX, identifies software vulnerabilities, which can then be patched or, in the hands of malicious actors, exploited.

This is not the first time the Commission has been targeted by a cyberattack.

In March, hackers compromised the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites, stealing around 91.7 GB of data. Earlier, in January, an attack on the Commission's central mobile-device infrastructure potentially exposed staff members' names and phone numbers.

The Italian company Bending Spoons agreed on Thursday to buy Mailchimp, the US email marketing platform, from Intuit for $3.68 billion (€3.35bn).

How Bending Spoons grew through acquisitions

Founded in 2013 in Copenhagen and now based in Milan, Bending Spoons has grown by acquiring other companies in the web services sector, then improving and relaunching their products. It has been listed on Nasdaq since 1 July 2026, with an IPO price of $29 a share.

German airline Lufthansa plans to axe 1,000 full-time jobs at its hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, after its core carrier lost €20 million a month on average between January and September, according to a letter to employees seen by AFP on Friday.

Strikes by pilots and cabin crew, and a surge in jet fuel prices since the Iran war began, have slowed its turnaround.

Launched in 2024, the turnaround plan includes more than 700 measures meant to lift earnings by €2.5 billion by 2028, but those announced to date are "no longer sufficient", the letter warned.

"The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation," the letter said.

It is unclear whether the 1,000 posts, about 2.5% of the airline's roughly 40,000 staff, are part of the 4,000 mostly administrative jobs Lufthansa Group said last year it would cut by 2030.

Mixed group results

The wider group, which also owns Swiss, Austrian Airlines and Brussels Airlines and is buying up to 49.9% of TAP Air Portugal in a €1.2 billion deal, has fared better.

Its operating profit, which excludes one-off items, rose 6% to €1.4bn in the third quarter, beating analysts' expectations on strong demand for premium long-haul seats.

Net profit, which includes one-off items, jumped 30% to €1.26bn, partly thanks to valuation gains and a tax charge that had weighed on the year-earlier figure.

Nine-month net profit was still down 35%, and on 3 November the group trimmed its full-year operating profit forecast to between €1.7bn and €2bn, from up to €2.2bn.

The core airline's third-quarter operating profit fell by a third to €300mn, and CEO Carsten Spohr said that "we must now accelerate the financial turnaround of our core brand".

From Pius XI's Mercedes to John Paul II's Popemobile: eight historic cars show how Popes' vehicles have changed. The Vatican Museums exhibition retraces a century of history, between technology, curiosities and safety.

There once was a pope who could tell his driver when to accelerate, when to slow down and even when to return to the Vatican, simply by pressing a button. Another, by contrast, had a car turned into an open-top vehicle so that he could be seen more clearly by the crowd. And then there was John Paul II, who had a barber's chair adapted as a papal seat, so that he could greet the faithful.

The cars of popes tell a story that goes far beyond engines, bodywork and comfort. They reveal the character of the pontiffs, the way they choose to be among people and, above all, how communication of the papacy has changed - from the solemnity of limousines to the search for direct contact with the faithful, and the growing need to protect those who travel under the spotlight.

This is the journey traced by the exhibition "A century of Popemobiles", that's now on at the Vatican Museums (source in Italian). Eight historic Mercedes-Benz cars retrace almost 100 years of papal mobility. They are accompanied by a Benz Patent-Motorwagen from 1886, considered the first car in history, and a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class, broadening the view of how the automobile has evolved.

Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Vatican Museums historical collections says each vehicle has its own story: "The message is very simple: papal mobility exists so that the pope can draw close to everyone, all over the world. The use of cars is not just about moving the Pontiff around within Vatican City".

We have seen this too in the most recent images of apostolic journeys: the Pope crossing cities and, from the moment after he steps off the plane, being able to make himself visible, bless people and ensure there is direct contact with the people of God.

A story in which each pontiff has, in one way or another, left his mark, including by choosing how he wished to be transported.

Pius XI, the Pope who fell in love with his car

The relationship between Mercedes-Benz and the Vatican officially begins in 1930, when Pius XI receives a Nürburg 460 (W 08), a large limousine donated by the German car manufacturer. It is the first Mercedes regularly used by a pope.

Achille Ratti, elected in 1922, was a man of culture, a scholar and lover of the mountains, with a past as a mountaineer and explorer. A Pontiff accustomed to looking far ahead, who did not shun the innovations of his time. The car also became a tool for leaving the Vatican, after the long period of the so-called imprisonment of the popes, which began with the end of the Papal States in 1870.

The Nürburg 460 is far from a standard official car: the interior is customised with a single seat for the pope, upholstered in fine silk brocade, selected woods, metallic detailing and a decorated ceiling. A kind of travelling sitting room, designed to underline the prestige of the papal figure.

But it is not just a question of luxury. Some papal cars from that era had a 'backseat driver' function panel, allowing the pope to instruct the chauffeur using buttons labelled "Forward", "Slow", "Right" and "Return to the Vatican". A sort of remote control before its time.

John XXIII, the "good Pope" who opens the windows

The pope's public presence also changed with John XXIII. Angelo Roncalli, a.ka. the "good Pope", had an informal style, a cheerful manner and a natural ability to relate to people. His pontificate, shaped by the Second Vatican Council, led the Church into a period of greater dialogue and openness.

The cars began to follow this transformation as well. In 1960, the Mercedes 300 d Landaulet (W 189) arrived, with rear windows that can be completely removed to allow the pope to be seen more easily and better greet people during public outings.

The features are already those of a vehicle built around the needs of the most important passenger: an electrically adjustable central seat, controls for the air conditioning and communications within easy reach, automatic steps to make it easier to get in and out of the vehicle.

Mercedes seems to have understood that the pope's car must not only take him to his destination: it must also allow him to meet people along the way.

Paul VI, the travelling Pope who invents the papamobile

If there is one pontiff who turned travel into a fundamental part of papal communication, it is Paul VI. Giovanni Battista Montini is the first modern pope to travel by plane and to make a series of international apostolic journeys, reaching places never before visited by a pontiff.

In 1964 he flew to the Holy Land, then to India in 1965, and in the following years to other continents. His mission was to reach the faithful in Rome and beyond by going to their countries to meet people and let them see him up close.

His Mercedes 600 Pullman Landaulet (W 100) from 1965 has a roof that opens at the rear specifically so that the pontiff can greet the crowds.

In 1967, a Mercedes 300 SEL Pullman (W 109) also arrives, another of the cars that mark the evolution of papal automobiles.

But the birth of the modern papamobile is above all linked to a practical need. As Barbagallo explains, "up until Paul VI, and then also with John Paul I, who as we all know had a very brief pontificate, the Pope went to audiences and even entered the Paul VI Audience Hall on a sedia gestatoria".

Paul VI, who found himself celebrating the Jubilee of 1975, was the first to realise that with the sedia gestatoria he could no longer make circuits around St Peter's Square, so he arranged for an open-top car to be purchased

That first vehicle was still a production car made available to the Pontiff. But it marked a decisive change: the Pope no longer simply had to be transported, he could now cross the square and be seen by all the pilgrims.

To grasp the difference between the traditional papal saloons and the papamobiles, Barbagallo retraces the evolution of these vehicles: "The way they have developed has constantly highlighted, on the one hand, the Pope's comfort, on the other his security, and on yet another the fact that the Pope can be seen. In saloons, that is the black cars, the Pope is only seen by those on his side of the vehicle, whereas in a papamobile he can be seen equally from the right, the left, the front or the back. That, of course, is what creates the difference between the two means of transport".

John Paul II, the Pope of the crowds and the barber's chair

With John Paul II, the popemobile became an icon. Karol Wojtyła was a pope with a strong physical presence, used to direct contact, long international journeys and vast crowds. Before becoming Pope he was an actor, poet, sports enthusiast and lover of the mountains. It is no surprise that he was not especially drawn to the idea of remaining seated in a closed limousine.

From the beginning he refused to use the traditional sedia gestatoria, the ceremonial chair on which popes were carried during ceremonies. He preferred a motor vehicle that allowed him to move around and greet people freely.

This is where one of the most curious episodes in the history of popemobiles comes in: for some of the first open vehicles a swivelling barber's chair was adapted, mounted on a metal base. A decidedly unusual seat for the head of the Catholic Church, but practical in allowing him to turn and greet the crowd from every side.

The Mercedes that fixed the image of the modern popemobile in the public imagination arrived in 1980, for John Paul II's trip to Germany. It is a 230 G (W 460), based on the G-Class, with a raised seat and a large transparent dome at the rear. The Pope can be seen from every side while remaining protected from the weather.

On 13 May 1981, however, the attempted assassination in St Peter's Square changed everything. From that moment the pope's safety became a central concern and the popemobiles were gradually fitted with bullet-proof protection.

As Barbagallo recalls, "that first popemobile was, of course, a standard production car given for the Pope's use; it had no comforts and no particular safety features. But from then on there was an evolution that, sadly, is also closely linked to the attack in St Peter's Square on John Paul II, after which heavily armoured popemobiles began to be used, as they still are today".

The G-Class became one of the most recognisable models of his pontificate. In 1997, a long-wheelbase Mercedes S 500 Landaulet (series 140) also joined the fleet, with a hydraulically operated rear soft top and a large seat for the pope.

In 2002 the Mercedes ML 430 "Popemobile" (W 163) was added to the history of papal vehicles, another off-roader adapted to the pontiff's needs.

Benedict XVI, technology and the search for protection

With Benedict XVI the style changes again. Joseph Ratzinger, a theologian and intellectual, has a more reserved approach than his predecessor's stage presence, but maintains the tradition of close encounters with the faithful.

In 2012, the Mercedes ML 500 "Popemobile" (W 166) arrives, with larger glass surfaces to improve visibility and reduce the sense of separation between the pope and the people.

It is a popemobile that attempts to reconcile two needs that have become inseparable: protection and proximity. The pontiff must be visible, but must also be able to travel in safety.

A car that is more than just a car

Today, the popemobile is far more than a means of transport. As Leo XIV made clear at the inauguration of the exhibition, it has become a means of bringing the pontiff closer to people.

And there is a curious detail that illustrates how special the relationship with these vehicles is: the Pope's seat is unlike any other. Designed for him alone, every detail, from the position of the seat to the heated support bar, is suited to his needs.

Een the way a pope chooses to travel can say a great deal about how he chooses to be in the world.

The exhibition at the Vatican Museums, set up in the glass pavilion of the Giardino Quadrato, will remain open until 28 January 2027.

On the final day of COP31, one country says it will “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact, which requires consensus.

It’s crunch time as COP31 enters its final day of discussions, following a lacklustre draft deal that sparked heavy backlash.

The annual UN climate summit, which is being held in Antalya, Türkiye, may overrun into the weekend amid growing divisions.

Yesterday (19 November), co-host Australia unveiled a slimmed-down draft deal that removed all mentions of fossil fuels – the leading driver of climate change – despite growing momentum to publish an exit strategy.

It signals a repeat of the COP30 summit in Belém last year, where the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) was erased from the final deal following resistance from fossil-fuel exporting countries.

Panama threatens to block final COP31 deal

COP agreements require consensus from all parties – that’s almost 200 nations – which means progress is often slow and incremental.

However, Panama appears to be putting its foot down, threatening to block any final deal that doesn’t deliver on a cap of oil production alongside a strident defence of science.

In a letter to COP31 hosts, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro said his country would “not join any consensus, and will formally object in the closing plenaries, to the adoption of any decision that does not lead to an outcome satisfactory” to its principles and values.

Navarro added that Panama would “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact.

Earlier this week, the politician argued that the world is being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and that nations are “in love with its kidnappers”.

We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.

“They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

TAFF roadmaps gain appeal outside of the UN remit

Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, but language around energy sources is highly contested at the yearly talks.

However, following the first TAFF conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, which took place in April, several countries have established their own exit strategy – with Europe leading the way.

Before COP31, France, Germany and the Netherlands published national roadmaps to get away from coal, oil and gas.

On 11 November, two days into the talks, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF.

Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.

While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.

What will COP31 actually decide?

Experts have criticised the erasure of fossil fuels from the latest draft deal, warning that the talks risk becoming a “ghost COP”.

"The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here,” Mohamed Adow, founder and director of climate think tank Power Shift Africa said on Thursday, 19 November.

“After the progress made in 2023 at COP28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all.

“COP31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis.”

Inga Fritzen Buan from environmental group WWF told news agency AFP that some major fossil energy producers are attempting to “undermine” everything related to emissions cuts and the energy transition.

“With this draft, they’re succeeding,” Buan added. “This is not a mere disagreement over the placement of a comma.”

Electrification takes centre stage

The latest text included a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 – a key initiative of Türkiye.

However, concern remains that the draft deal does not explicitly require that extra electricity be powered by clean energy rather than coal or gas.

“We are going to fight for clean electrification” met by renewables and nuclear energy, French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters.

Some countries rejected calls to ramp up carbon capture, utilisation and storage technology, which critics see as an expensive distraction from cutting pollution.

The draft also proposes further discussions toward “tripling” finance for climate adaptation measures by 2035, but drops a $120 billion (approximately €109 billion) goal being sought by developing nations.

Rich nations have long resisted calls to increase support for countries struggling to adapt to climate change, citing budget constraints and insisting that big emerging economies such as China also contribute.

The draft deal also contains a recognition of the “best-available science” and a reference to the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), a key battleground at COP31.

Brussels is incorporating military fuel needs into the planning and assessment of national emergency oil stocks, according to a document seen by Euronews.

The European Commission wants EU governments to look beyond emergency oil stockpiles to secure enough diesel, jet fuel and other oil products to keep essential services and military operations running during a prolonged crisis, according to a draft document seen by Euronews.

More than half of EU countries (61.54%) reported trouble ensuring sufficient fuel access when armed forces move across the continent in a 2025 Commission impact assessment, posing a major hurdle for the bloc's plans for military readiness by 2030.

With Russia's war against Ukraine at its border and a series of hybrid attacks sweeping the continent over the past weeks, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius recently warned that the EU needs to prepare for a substantial increase in military fuel consumption during a conflict.

He noted that in the event of a war outbreak, NATO could need to move and sustain 100,000 troops during the first ten days of a crisis, stressing the importance of diesel and jet fuel for military operations.

The EU's new approach to energy security deems it crucial to place oil supplies within the EU's wider defence and strategy preparedness agenda to "prevent or minimise risks" on a range of measures.

According to the draft document, which lays out an overhaul of the Commission's oil security rules, national governments would need to assess how much emergency fuel they hold and whether their refineries, ports, pipelines and distribution networks could withstand major disruptions.

"Inadequacy between the evolution of consumption, including military demand, and the evolution of the fuel supply chain, including along military mobility corridors," reads the paper, referring to assessments expected by EU governments.

Under the draft rules, EU countries would have to factor military demand into their national risk assessments, including the possibility of sudden increases in fuel requirements and simultaneous pressure from civilian and military consumers.

A recent NATO energy security study found that the EU's ability to fuel its armed forces could be undermined by a shrinking refinery industry, growing dependence on foreign suppliers and insufficient jet fuel reserves.

"Jet fuel is precisely the product on which NATO Europe is structurally short. It is also the fuel most likely to retain (or even grow) its demand to 2050, and the product with the least amount of stock cover at 49 days," reads the study.

NATO's study noted that Europe imports between 27% and 30% of its jet fuel from outside the region, leaving it exposed to foreign suppliers.

Dependence is also highly concentrated — 36% of external imports come from one supplier, while three countries account for 65% of all external supplies.

Assessing refinery's capacity

While EU governments are pursuing industrial decarbonisation, strategically important refining capacity is disappearing, raising the question of whether the bloc's refinery industry is becoming a national security liability.

Despite the efforts to accelerate the energy transition, the new energy security framework puts considerable attention on refineries — an industry sector in decline across Europe over the past nearly two decades.

"We need to counter this trend and ensure that we have adequate and flexible refining capacity in Europe. Today and for the future. This is not just a matter of economic competitiveness. It is also a matter of security," the Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said after a dialogue on refineries alongside Defense Commissioner Kubilius.

Even if EU countries have access to crude oil alone, they need sufficient capacity to turn it into the diesel, gasoline and jet fuel required by transport, industry and defence.

According to the draft document, national authorities would have to identify their refineries, assess their production capacity and report major closures, expansions and planned investments.

Brussels also expects capitals to examine the consequences of losing critical infrastructure and becoming overly dependent on a limited number of foreign suppliers.

The document suggests the Commission is asking governments to consider whether allowing domestic refining capacity to disappear could create a strategic vulnerability that can't easily be repaired if a crisis hits.

The draft would also require EU capitals to map their dependence on individual suppliers, including the countries from which they import crude oil, diesel, gasoline and jet fuel.

The goal is to assess how these dependencies could evolve over the next five years and what would happen if a major supplier suddenly stopped deliveries.

EU countries could face greater scrutiny over their emergency preparedness.

The draft document suggests that capitals would need to prepare national risk assessments and preparedness and response plans covering physical attacks, cyber threats, extreme weather, ownership of critical infrastructure and prolonged disruptions affecting several supply routes.

Collision course with clean transition

Environmental campaigners have argued that reviving refineries across the EU could slow down the bloc's goal to cut CO2 emissions at a time when a series of climate policies are being diluted.

The softening of the EU's carbon market and the CO2 emissions car rules, alongside the delay in implementing methane rules, raises questions over whether Brussels will reach its 2040 climate target to ultimately become carbon neutral by 2050.

Despite seeking to boost electrification and reduce oil consumption, Brussels recognises that armed forces will continue to need reliable supplies of diesel and jet fuel, including during sudden increases in military demand.

The Commission is expected to unveil its proposal to revise oil security supply rules on 2 December.

"I'm not sure we have a common acceptance of Article 5," Zelenskyy said on Thursday evening after a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.

"What does it mean?"

The idea of developing a security guarantee for Ukraine modelled under NATO's collective defence, which states that an armed attack against one ally shall be considered an attack against all of them, was first raised in December of last year. However, the proposal was never fully developed as peace negotiations subsequently stalled.

It came back into focus on Thursday, as European leaders gathered in Berlin.

US special envoy Jared Kushner, who took part in the meeting, said President Donald Trump was "open" to providing such a commitment to a post-war Ukraine.

"From an American perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," Kushner said, speaking next to Zelenskyy.

"Obviously, it has to be in America's interest to do that. And we also have to make sure that it's part of a broader security package."

Kushner claimed that Russia has become "comfortable" with the concept, though he admitted "there's a lot of scepticism and disbelief" about it in Moscow. Kushner also said the Russian intention is "to not have another war in the future".

"That's why it's important to restart the dialogue between Europe and Russia," he said.

"We have to work on a system of incentives and interests to make sure that whatever agreement we come to is something that will be kept, it will be monitored, there'll be huge deterrence, and there'll be massive consequences if it's ever violated."

But in a subsequent press conference, Zelenskyy challenged the vagueness of Kushner's response, asking for specific details such as the possible deployment of US troops or the establishment of US bases on Ukrainian soil.

"What about American soldiers?" he said. "Do you have an answer on it? Me not. For today. I don't know the answer."

For an Article 5-like guarantee to work in practice, he said, the US and Europe have to properly spell out how they would react to a new Russian assault.

"What will partners do?" he said. "What happens if – sorry to be sceptical – not if, but when (Russians) will try to do it again? What will they do?"

"It has to be clear not only to partners (but also) to people, societies, investors" who will come to Ukraine after the war, he went on.

"All these people, they need clear answers."

Zelenskyy said that full-time NATO membership, a long-held goal for Kyiv and a red line for Moscow, would make it clearer, as his country would automatically benefit from the real Article 5 provision, the linchpin of the alliance's deterrence.

Ukraine's NATO dream has split allies, with some arguing it would be the easiest way to avoid a new invasion and others warning it would unnecessarily provoke Russia.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that Russia's "maximalist" demands warranted revisiting "the question of Ukraine's NATO accession".

The meeting in Berlin ended with a declaration signed by Germany, France and the UK that featured a subtle reference to a potential Article 5-like security guarantee.

The text did not describe it as such, but as "a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security in the case of a future armed attack by Russia".

House prices are soaring across Europe as supply falls short of demand. With three days of coordinated protests due to begin on Friday in several countries, governments are under growing pressure to make housing more affordable.

House prices have surged by almost 70% in the EU since 2015, and rents have climbed by 25%, far outstripping income growth, according to the bloc's statistics office, Eurostat.

Costs have risen the most in Portugal, followed by the Netherlands.

Rising housing costs have helped fuel a wave of protests across Europe. Housing rights groups and trade unions from France, the UK, Belgium, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Greece have called for three days of coordinated action from Friday, 20 November. They are demanding that governments guarantee the right to housing and bring down housing, food and energy costs.

Governments across Europe have announced measures ranging from rent caps and tighter rules on short-term lets to plans to build more affordable homes, as rising prices and a shortage of homes squeeze renters and buyers.

Here is a look at the measures being taken to ease the burden.

Spain

The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her lifelong home in September sparked a national uproar that led parliament to pass new laws restricting evictions and property speculation.

But lawmakers rejected the automatic renewal of tenancy agreements, a main demand of protesters, and the conservative Popular Party, which leads in opinion polls, has vowed to repeal the measures if it takes power after the 29 November general election.

The left-wing government had already passed a law in 2023 calling for more social housing and rent controls in regions where the housing crisis was most acute.

But the measures have been applied only sporadically so far.

Barcelona, one of the most visited cities in Europe, has pledged to get more flats on the market by not renewing the roughly 10,000 permits for tourist rentals on Airbnb and other sites.

Portugal

The centre-right government of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro has focused on tax measures to encourage owners to put their homes or flats on the rental market.

He has also raised taxes on property purchases by non-residents.

But in September, lawmakers approved a rental market overhaul that makes it easier and quicker to evict tenants who do not pay their rent, sparking a wave of protests.

The Netherlands

The government of one of Europe's most densely populated countries set rent caps for many privately owned homes.

But many owners preferred to sell instead, leaving fewer homes available to rent, while rents for properties outside the cap continued to rise.

Earlier this year, the government announced new measures aimed at speeding up housing construction while guaranteeing that two-thirds of the new homes would be kept affordable for buyers and renters.

France

Since 2023, the centrist government has promised a "supply shock" with measures to encourage the construction of new homes and get more homes onto the rental market, including by easing environmental rules.

One bill currently under discussion in parliament would relax rules forcing owners to improve poorly insulated homes before they can be rented out.

The far right wants the insulation rules scrapped altogether.

The bill would also streamline the rules on home construction and provide bigger tax breaks to private landlords.

Germany

A lack of affordable rental properties in Germany has led to a revival in housing cooperatives, member-owned associations that offer an alternative to both renting and ownership.

Residents buy shares in the cooperative, which owns and manages the housing, and pay fees for their flats, helping to keep costs down and protect tenants from speculation.

Cooperatives now manage around 10% of Germany's rental stock.

Since 2010, rents on new leases have been capped in regions where housing markets are tightest, which has reined in prices but led to a decline in new home construction.

The left-wing party Die Linke made Berlin's housing crisis a rallying cry in recent local elections, promising to expropriate tens of thousands of flats owned by corporate landlords, a move the central government is trying to block.

Britain

The Labour government wants to increase supply by creating 300,000 social homes while also providing financial help for first-time buyers.

It has also banned no-fault evictions and limited rent increases to once a year.

But high interest rates, along with tax and regulatory burdens, continue to limit the construction of new homes needed to ease the chronic shortage.

Italy

Protests have led the government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to lower taxes on rental income, a move aimed at encouraging more owners to put homes and flats on the market.

It plans to make around 100,000 more homes available over the next 10 years, either by renovating existing social housing or building new homes, while simplifying regulatory procedures.

Greece

Authorities have focused on limiting the surge in short-term rentals in one of Europe's top tourist destinations, in particular in Athens and Thessaloniki.

The government has also reined in its "golden visa" programme for foreigners who buy property, which critics say has taken homes off the market for Greeks.

Subsidies provide lower-interest mortgages for first-time buyers, and public funds are also available for owners who commit to long-term rentals after renovating their properties.

Crews have been assigned to the tankers, Iranian flags have been raised over them, and Tehran plans to send them in convoy toward the Sea of Oman exit in the coming days, the reports said.

Ship-tracking firm TankerTrackers said available data confirmed Iran was resuming oil exports.

Satellite imagery and shipping data showed the transfers took place near Kharg Island with automatic identification systems (AIS) switched off to conceal the oil's origin. Washington had previously warned it would target vessels involved in such operations.

Israel's Channel 14 and Sabereen News, an outlet close to Iran-backed armed groups, reported that dozens of Iranian tankers were preparing to head towards China and were moving closer to the blockade lines.

Mohammad Enayati Najafabadi, in a post on X resharing a piece by Iran's state-affiliated Fars news agency, warned that disrupting an Iranian tanker's route "will lead to explosions at the oil facilities of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain," which he described as a personal analysis.

The US had been moving more oil through the Strait of Hormuz and exporting more refined products — petrol, diesel and jet fuel — for several weeks, he said, claiming supply had actually risen.

The EU and UK agreed on a youth scheme letting 100,000 young people live in each other’s territory, but a deal on how much to lower university fees was delayed by six months.

Brussels and London have agreed to let 100,000 young Europeans live in the UK, but a deal on university fees has been postponed by six months, at a major summit on Friday.

The EU and the UK have been seeking a broader reset in relations at their second bilateral summit since Brexit, and a youth mobility scheme to live and study abroad is one of its main elements.

“This is something which is important in terms of people-to-people contacts on both sides of the channel,” an EU official said.

The Youth Experience Scheme (YES) will allow 100,000 young people from the EU and 100,000 from the UK to live in each other’s territory for up to three years. It is expected to be up and running by January 2030 at the latest.

However, the two sides failed to settle the contentious issue of university fees, committing instead to hash out a deal within six months.

The UK, which hosts far more EU students than it sends to the bloc, wants to simply lower the fees.

The EU, by contrast, wants its students to be treated equally to British ones at UK universities, as they did before Brexit, when EU students benefited from equal treatment under EU rules prohibiting discrimination on grounds of nationality.

The post-Brexit rise in fees has driven EU enrolment down sharply. The number of EU students starting a course at UK universities fell by 57% between 2020/21 and 2023/24, according to the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory.

“Since Brexit, the level of students from both sides studying on the other side has decreased, notably EU students in the UK. We think that this is something that makes our relationship poorer, and we want to address this,” the EU official added.

The UK has already agreed to rejoin Erasmus+, the EU exchange programme for education and vocational training, with participation starting on 1 January 2027.

Besides the youth scheme, the EU and the UK also agreed several other deals, including aligning agrifood standards and linking their carbon markets.

The question is whether member states will make final approval of these agreements conditional on a satisfactory deal on tuition fees.

Now that we know the identity of the seventh 007, it's time to go through all 25 Bond films and rank them from worst to best... Results may surprise you.

What a week it's been for all things Bond...

We finally have our new 007, with Robert Pattinson officially confirmed to don the tuxedo handed down from Daniel Craig.

The 40-year-old British actor now enters an exclusive club, featuring a character who has survived SPECTRE assassinations, shark attacks, studio bankrupcy, COVID, alcoholism, and presumably mulitple STDs. Oh, and persisted despite the fact they didn't manage to release a Bond film in 2007 - that marketing just wrote itself...

Since it's still too early to know how Pattinson will put his mark on 007 and what an Amazon-produced Bond film looks like, now seems like a good time to look back on the legacy of the longest lasting film franchise of all time, and rank all the 25 Bond films once and for all.

(For you pedants out there, yes, Godzilla is technically the longest lasting film series, but as a continuous main series, Bond still comes first.)

From Dr. No to No To Time To Die, bypassing non-canonical entries Casino Royale (1967) and Never Say Never Again (1983), here are the results – which will doubtlessly infuriate some Bond fans...

25. Diamonds Are Forever (1971)

In a nutshell: Sean Connery's last (official) mission sees him follow the trace of diamond smugglers, head to Las Vegas, and attempt to foil Blofeld's plans on an oil rig. It's a disaster from start to finish.

Pros: A stellar title song; Charles Gray is a decent Blofeld... That's about it.

Cons: Overly campy yet somehow lifeless; Connery is out of shape and his toupee is doing most of the acting; utterly vacuous female protagonists; offensively stereotypical gay henchmen Mr. Wint and Mr. Kidd; the worst script the franchise has ever known.

Key moment: The title song by Shirley Bassey.

24. Die Another Day (2002)

In a nutshell: Pierce Brosnan's fourth and final turn as 007 is one of the most groanworthy Bond films in the series. It sees Bond face off against Gustav Graves (Toby Stephens), a North Korean general who gets a Western makeover through gene therapy and who's all about the diamonds. Seriously, diamonds are the kiss of death for Bond.

Pros: Bond getting captured and tortured in North Korea; the fact that Die Another Day was so awful it forced producers to take a long hard look in the mirror and reboot the franchise with Casino Royale.

Cons: Where to begin? The invisible car; the questionable whitewashing; the ice palace; giant lasers; naff CGI; that moment Bond surfs on an iceberg; Madonna's disastrous theme song and cringey cameo; Halle Berry's dialogue... There are few redeeming qualities in this one.

Key moment: Judi Dench's M decommissioning Bond and telling him he's "no use to anyone now". How fitting.

23. The Man With The Golden Gun (1974)

In a nutshell: Roger Moore's James Bond faces off against Scaramanga, the world’s deadliest assassin, in a plot involving a solar enegry device adventurously called Solex... There's some martial arts in there too.

Pros: Christopher Lee as Scaramanga, who deserved better than to be stuck in Moore's second outing as Bond.

Cons: A third nipple as a key narrative plot point; Britt Ekland's character development reduced to being in a bikini all the time; the return of Sheriff Pepper after his already tiresome appearance in Live And Let Die; the last act on an island featuring Hervé Villechaize as Scaramanga's butler Nick Nack – meaning that it's essentially 007 on Fantasy Island.

Key moment: Christopher Lee assembling his golden gun and outclassing Bond at the dinner table.

22. Quantum Of Solace (2008)

In a nutshell: Picking up where Casino Royale left off, Daniel Craig returns as 007 in a revenge-fuelled mission in which a shady organisation named Quantum tries to control South American water reserves. Despite an effort amongst Bond fans to rehabilitate this outing, it remains a real step down from the franchise high of Craig's 2006 introduction as Bond.

Pros: Craig is great and looks the part; there's something to be said about the lean and mean execution; a lot of the film's shortcomings can be explained (forgiven?) by the fact the script wasn't finished because of the 2008 writers' strike.

Cons: A rubbish theme song by Jack White and Alicia Keys; lunatic editing which induces seizures and ruins the opening car chase and a promising face-off during a horse race; a janky script which doesn't know what to do with Mathieu Amalric's villain; the underwhelming climax in the desert.

Key moment: The final goodbye to Vesper Lynd in the film's closing moments.

21. Octopussy (1983)

In a nutshell: Roger Moore’s penultimate effort was Octopussy (stop giggling at the back), which sees him heading to India and West Germany as he tries to prevent the theft of a nuclear weapon. A Fabergé egg plays an important part in there somewhere.

Pros: A decent premise featuring a murdered 00 agent; the antagonists played by Louis Jordan and Steven Beroff are great fun; Maud Adams is - and always will be - perfect.

Cons: The of-its-time exoticism; Roger Moore swinging on vines and doing a Tarzan yell; Roger Moore in a crocodile costume; Roger Moore in a gorilla costume; Roger Moore in a clown costume.

Key moment: The climax at Octopussy's palace. Stop it with the snickering.

20. Spectre (2015)

In a nutshell: As the title suggests, the ring-wearing Illuminati are back and seeking to control the flow of information by placing agents at the heart of intelligence services around the world. To ensure world domination, they're also orchestrating terrorist attacks. How could something so promising go so wrong?

Pros: The Day of the Dead opener; a strong first half.

Cons: Destroying all the promising elements - from hamfistedly retconning the previous Daniel Craig films in a bid to create a Bond cinematic universe, to ruining the character of Blofeld (Christoph Waltz) by making him Bond's adoptive brother. Worse, his motivation boils down to unresolved daddy issues. It's complete Austin Powers. The only way it could have worked was by making Waltz SPECTRE's "Number One" and revealing that the otherwise wasted Monica Bellucci was in fact the one pulling the strings as the head of SPECTRE. Now that would have been a twist. Oh, and Radiohead were supposed to do the theme song and their stellar effort was ditched in favour of Sam Smith's forgettable ballad.

Key moment: That "one-shot" Mexico opening and the ensuing helicopter fight is killer. Pity the rest topples into convoluted nonsense.

19. Moonraker (1979)

In a nutshell: Bond goes to space in this Star Wars-influenced mission about the theft of a space shuttle and the creation of a master race. Frequently cited as one of the worst Bond films, it's actually an enjoyable jump-the-shark romp.

Pros: Michel Lonsdale as megalomaniac Hugo Drax; most of the camp done right – except the gondola chase in Venice, which is just plain Looney Tunes.

Cons: The laser battle in space; Jaws (Richard Kiel) getting a girlfriend (Blanche Ravalec); an outlandish plot which forgets that Bond is an MI6 agent and not Luke Skywalker's opposite number.

Key moment: Ah, to hell with it, we're actually quite chuffed for Jaws and his new squeeze. Good for those two.

18. You Only Live Twice (1967)

In a nutshell: Bond tries to find out who is stealing American and Soviet spacecrafts out of orbit. Spoiler: it's Blofeld, who resides in a massive volcano lair. 007 heads to Japan to team up with his ninja counterparts to stop the cat-stroking madman.

Pros: Bond faking his own death; Ken Adam's volcanic lair; Donald Pleasance as Blofeld.

Cons: Sean Connery's yellowface makeover; more racist caricatures and sexist stereotypes than you can shake a Martini shaker at; the feeling that after a great run of four films for Connery with Dr. No, From Russia With Love, Goldfinger and Thunderball, this is when the Bond franchise started to show it could run out of steam.

Key moment: Blofeld killing one of his agents by dumping her in a vat full of piranhas. You've got to admire the nefarious bastardry inherent to his interior designing skills.

17. The World Is Not Enough (1999)

In a nutshell: Pierce Brosnan's third go as Bond confirmed that his run got progressively worse as it went on. Still, this movie isn't all bad, as it sees terrorist Renard (an underserved Robert Carlyle) blowing up some oil pipelines, tormenting his past kidnap victim Elektra (Sophie Marceau) and looking to get his hands on some plutonium.

Pros: Sophie Marceau revealed as the Stockholm Syndrome-suffering true villain, becoming the franchise's first female big bad; Garbage's title song; a strong opening that struck the right balance between serious and camp.

Cons: Denise Richards as nuclear physicist Dr Christmas Jones; the niggling sensation that Brosnan is trying to keep things serious while the script won't allow him to; that final joke before the credits roll, which makes even the most dedicated Bond fan want to jump head-first into Blofeld's piranha vat.

Key moment: That fitting farewell to Desmond Llewelyn, who played Q from 1963 to 1999.

16. A View To A Kill (1985)

In a nutshell: Not the best of endings for Roger Moore, as he went out with A View To Kill, which is frequently voted one of the franchise's worst instalments. Still, it isn't that bad and works a kitschy 80s throwback. Will Bond be able to stop Max Zorin (Christopher Walken), an evil Nazi eugenics experiment turned microchip mogul working for the Russians, from destroying Silicon Valley?

Pros: Two scenery-chewing villains courtesy of Walken and Grace Jones; the Duran Duran song is better than you remember; you end up rooting for the Silicon Valley genocide to work.

Cons: Moore looks shagged out and the stunt performers are visibly taking over; the Beach Boys needle-drop during the snowboarding sequence; Tanya Roberts and all her screaming; the general low-energy feel.

Key moment: Christopher Walken being manic and one of the best antagonists of the series.

15. Live And Let Die (1973)

In a nutshell: Moore’s debut as 007 was decent but it has aged terribly. The actor makes his mark on Bond as a cooler, more playful Bond; but he's heading to Harlem to uncover a heroin operation... Cue: A product of the times instalment, which also features Jane Seymour as a tarot-reading fortune teller.

Pros: A promising start for Moore; the voodoo stuff works as cover for the drug smuggling / distributing; the music is great; some inventive deaths; Yaphet Kotto makes for a fantastic villain.

Cons: The misguided blacksploitation angle leading to some uncomfortable racist stereotypes; the introduction of Louisiana Sheriff J.W. Pepper (Clifton James); Bond rigging a card deck to steal Solitaire's virginity - a creepy low point for the character, even by 007's dubious standards.

Key moment: Geoffrey Holder as the sinister Baron Samedi and Yaphet Kotto acting his socks off.

14. Tomorrow Never Dies (1997)

In a nutshell: Brosnan's second Bond film was released alongside Titanic, so it took a beating at the box office. However, Tomorrow Never Dies has aged rather well in telling the story of a villainous press mogul Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) who seeks to dictate the world’s rolling news coverage by orchestrating criminal acts and manipulating headlines. It's essentially Bond vs Rupert Murdoch.

Pros: A prescient story about pre-"fake news" media manipulation and Chinese expansionist plans; the incomparable Michelle Yeoh kicking more arse than 007 as Wai Lin; a fun bunch of villains, including two sadistic German baddies Dr. Kaufman and Jaws-throwback Stamper.

Cons: An underpowered theme song from Sheryl Crow; a miscast Jonathan Pryce as Carver, who was originally going to be played by Anthony Hopkins; Teri Hatcher doing her level best.

Key moment: Dr. Kaufman (Vincent Schiavelli) stealing the show as the doctor who could shoot Bond "from Stuttgart und still create zee proper effect!"

13. Thunderball (1965)

In a nutshell: The fourth Bond film was released at the peak of Bondmania. Until Skyfall came along, Thunderball was the highest grossing 007 movie (adjusted for inflation), and it still stands as a tightly-paced thriller. It sees Bond try to stop SPECTRE's eye-patch wearing Largo from stealing nuclear warheads in a bid to blow up major cities in the US and UK. Another day at the office...

Pros: The iconic jetpack escape; SPECTRE's explosive boardroom shenanigans; we finally get to see all the 00 agents in one room; Claudine Auger's Domino and Luciana Paluzzi's Fiona Volpe holding their own against Bond and proving that swaggering male ego only gets you so far; SHARKS!

Cons: All the underwater stuff in the last act gets a bit boring; Tom Jones' bombastic but annoying theme song; all the Moneypenny flirting clearly shows MI6 doesn't have a competent HR department.

Key moment: Domino becomes the first female protagonist in the series to kill the villain and save Bond.

12. No Time To Die (2021)

In a nutshell: Endlessly delayed by COVID, Daniel Craig's final go was worth the wait. Granted, it still twists itself into knots with convoluted continuity from the previous adventures, and crams in far too much. But No Time To Die remains a bold and fitting swansong for Craig, who was the face of a rejuvinated franchise. In this one, Bond unretires and is on the trail of Safin (Rami Malek), who has stolen an off-the-books biological weapon from MI6.

Pros: Ana de Armas; strong action sequences; Craig proving that he'll be a very tough act to follow; the gut-punch finale; did we mention Ana de Armas?

Cons: An undercooked and poorly written villain; the overstuffed plot which loses momentum in the second half; an over-reliance on nostalgic callbacks.

Key moment: The surprisingly affecting finale which dares to kill off Bond for the first time. As such, it neatly caps off the Broccoli tenureship. Dr. No to No Time To Die : 1962 – 2021. Over to you, Amazon. Best of luck. And don't cock it up.

11. Dr. No (1962)

In a nutshell: Bond begins! The first Bond film is still one of the best and has aged surprisingly well compared to some others. We meet 007 for the first time - a suave and brutal agent who doesn't mind a quip and a flirt while he's saving the world and downing one too many beverages. The story sends him to Jamaica to investigate the murder of a fellow agent. There, he comes up against SPECTRE agent Dr. No, who likes shooting down American rockets in a bid to heat up the Cold War.

Pros: The Monty Norman-themed introduction; Connery nailing it on the first try and proving that Bond needs to be played by an unknown, as opposed to then-studio favourite Cary Grant; Ursula Andress and Joseph Wiseman both excellent as Honey Rider and Dr. No, respectively; the first Bond villain lair.

Cons: Pacing issues; a few editing gaffs; a formula still in need of a polish.

Key moment: Connery intoning “Bond. James Bond” while lighting a cigarette in a casino. A cinematic icon is born.

10. For Your Eyes Only (1981)

In a nutshell: Following Moonraker 's campy space antics, For Your Eyes Only was a bid to dial back the excesses and get back to a more grounded mission. And it worked - making this one a real standout in Moore’s run as Bond. For his 12th mission, 007 rushes to recover a MacGuffin weapons system, ATAC, before the Soviets get their hands on it. In doing so, he crosses paths with two warring clans led by Kristaos (Julian Glover) and Columbo (Topol), as well as Melina (Carole Bouquet) - a crossbow-wielding woman seeking to avenge the murder of her parents.

Pros: The high camp is gone and this back-to-basics approach feels more like a Cold War thriller rather than an end-of-the-world flick; the dialled down set pieces; the theme of revenge works; Topol is great as the pistachio-loving Columbo; a great climax in a Greek monastery.

Cons: Bond unceremoniously dropping Blofield down a chimney at the start; the parasol escape; Margaret Thatcher showing up at the end. Shudder.

Key moment: The death of Lisl (Cassandra Harris, who was Pierce Brosnan's first wife) on the beach and Bond pushing assassin Locque (Michael Gothard) off a cliff. Both sequences showed what Moore could do as an actor when he wasn't being asked to act with his eyebrows.

9. Licence To Kill (1989)

In a nutshell: Bond goes rogue in Timothy Dalton's second and final Bond adventure. It's a darker and nastier movie, which dared to up the violence. It was ahead of its time, as Dalton's turn as 007 was the blueprint for Craig's more gritty portrayal. Sadly, Licence To Kill (originally titled "Licence Revoked" but changed because American audiences associated the term with driving licences) was met with a polarized response, but it remains a standout. As for the plot: Ruthless drug kingpin Franz Sanchez (Robert Davi) kills Felix Leiter's wife and feeds Bond's CIA buddy to sharks. 007 has a debt and retaliates...

Pros: The personal stakes; a hard-hitting execution; Robert Davi and a young Benicio Del Toro acing their sadistic villain duties; Dalton proving he remains the most underrated Bond, as well as the proto-Craig.

Cons: It often feels like a great action-thriller rather than a Bond film; the legal rows which caused a six-year hiatus and ended up with Dalton quitting.

Key moment: Q showing up in the field to help Bond.

8. Skyfall (2012)

In a nutshell: When a cyber-terrorist with ties to M's past leaks the identities of agents around the world and blows up part of MI6, Bond comes out of self-imposed exile to save the day and his boss... Seeking to redeem the black mark of Quantum Of Solace, the Bond producers drafted director Sam Mendes to helm what would become a critical darling and the most commercially successful Bond film of all time. It was the fourteenth film to pass the billion-dollar mark.

Pros: Adele's Oscar-winning theme song; Bond left for dead in a compromised mission; Javier Bardem having a scene-stealing blast as Silva; Dench’s meatier role; Craig adding some emotional heft to a worn out Bond; a perfectly shot film by cinematographer Roger Deakins.

Cons: Some glaring plot holes in Silva's The Dark Knight -inspired escape plan; that godawful quip when Sévérine (Bérénice Marlohe) gets shot; the jarring Home Alone antics in the third act which undermine the rest of the film.

Key moment: Skyfall is the Dame Judi Dench show, and her farewell at the end is a real tear-jerker.

7. On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969)

In a nutshell: When Connery left the role after You Only Live Twice, he was replaced by an unknown Australian actor who had only been in a few commercials. George Lazenby's sole appearance as James Bond was once considered a massive misstep but has been reappraised by fans - including Christopher Nolan, who has singled it out as his favourite Bond film. OHMSS has Bond going undercover to flush out Blofeld (Telly Savalas) from his snowy hiding spot, all while falling in love with Countess Teresa "Tracy" di Vicenzo (Diana Rigg).

Pros: Peter Hunt's direction; the snowbound sequences; some visceral action scenes; Telly Savalas as the best Blofeld; Diana Rigg as the best Bond Girl ever; the tragic ending.

Cons: Lazenby can't shake off Connery's legacy, even if you get the impression he could have had he made more; that fourth-wall break in the opening scene; the swinging sex comedy antics with the patients in Blofeld's clinic; Lazenby in a kilt.

Key moment: That bold and unforgettable finale. Bond finally gets his happy ending and heads off to marital bliss... Only for Tracy to be executed in the car.

6. GoldenEye (1995)

In a nutshell: After a six-year post-Dalton hiatus due to legal woes, GoldenEye was the first post-Cold War Bond film, with Pierce Brosnan slipping into the tux. It was a critical and commercial triumph, with many praising director Martin Campbell for ushering in a new era for Bond – one which didn't reinvent the formula but updated it. It wouldn't be the last time Campbell revitalized 007, giving Bond a much-needed reboot in 2006 with Casino Royale ... GoldenEye sees our hero face off against presumed dead 006 (Sean Bean), who plans a daring hiest thanks to the titular MacGuffin.

Pros: Brosnan at his best and taking to the role of Bond like an olive to a chilled Vodka Martini; Judi Dench making her debut as M; Famke Janssen's Xenia Onatopp redefining safe sex; having a 00 agent go rogue; action sequences which include a jump from a dam and a tank chase in the streets of St. Petersberg.

Cons: An underwhelming ending; the gadget-filled car is set up but never gets used.

Key moment: M calling Bond a "sexist, misogynist dinosaur, a relic of the Cold War".

5. The Spy Who Loved Me (1977)

In a nutshell: After two middling films, it was third time lucky for Roger Moore, who hit his stride in the perfectly balanced and quintessential Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me. This finely tuned mission has it all: action, comedy, evil lairs, huge henchmen, a submarine car... The lot. Central to the plot is a missing microfilm, which leads MI6 and the KGB to team up. "Détente, indeed," as villain Karl Stromberg (Curd Jürgens) says.

Pros: One of the best damn Bond songs ever recorded; the iconic opening ski chase; Barbara Bach as Anya Amasova, Bond’s KGB counterpart; the introduction of the menacing Jaws (Richard Kiel); Moore finally owning Bond.

Cons: The soundtrack features some questionable guitar twangs which would have been more at home in a 70s porno.

Key moment: The skiing-off-a-cliff stunt soundtracked to the opening bars of Carly Simon's 'Nobody Does It Better'. Never equalled.

4. The Living Daylights (1987)

In a nutshell: Riot all you want, but it's a fact that The Living Daylights is the single most underrated and overlooked entry in the whole franchise. Many posit that GoldenEye saved Bond; but that honour goes to The Living Daylights. Having taken over from Moore, Timothy Dalton more than delivered the goods in his first turn as 007. His globetrotting mission takes him from London to eastern Europe, Morocco and Afghanistan, trying to uncover what links a rogue American warlord (Joe Don Baker), a supposed KGB defector (Jeroen Krabbé), and a cellist (Maryam d'Abo).

Pros: The assassinations during the opening training exercise; the underrated theme song by A-ha; the cello case snow chase shouldn't work but does; Bond confronting Pushkin (John Rhys-Davies) about the reactivation of the Smert Shpionam programme; a great finale; Dalton being the best Bond since Connery.

Cons: It's all killer no filler with this one. Deny it if you can.

Key moment: The moment Dalton turns his tux into a sniper's vest before picking up his rifle. Dangerous. Suave. Effortlessly cool.

3. Goldfinger (1964)

In a nutshell: Sean Connery's third entry was the one that set up and embraced everything the franchise became famous for – huge theme songs, outlandish plots, larger-than-life villains, the tricked out Aston Martin, female protagonists with ridiculous names... It's no mystery why Goldfinger is the first film that springs to mind when you're asked: "Picture a Bond movie."

Pros: The gold-painted woman; Oddjob's hat; that laser scene... Everything about Goldfinger made it a pop culture reference and one of the best Bonds. Special mention must go to Gert Fröbe as Auric Goldfinger, as well as the uncredited Michael Collins, who dubbed the German-born actor as his accent was too difficult to understand.

Cons: That completely unnecessary Beatles jab from Bond before he gets knocked out by Oddjob; the way Bond forces himself onto Pussy Galore (Honor Blackman) in the barn... Problematic doesn't even begin to cover it.

Key moment: "You ekssshhpect me to talk?” “No, Mr Bond, I expect you to DIE!”

2. Casino Royale (2006)

In a nutshell: He's too bland... He's too short... He's too blonde... When Daniel Craig was cast as Bond, everyone seemed to dismiss the casting decision as a massive misfire even before the actor had begun filming his first scene. Fast forward to the release of Casino Royale and all the naysayers were forced to eat a lot of humble pie. Martin Campbell came back to the director's chair after GoldenEye to ensure that everything went off without a hitch, and the results were plain to see. This was an exciting and gritty origin story that deconstructed Bond before he was fully formed as the agent we'd known before. More than that, Casino Royale was a perfect Bond film, featuring the best James Bond yet.

Pros: From the black-and-white opener showing how Bond got his 00 status all the way to the Venice showdown, via Chris Cornell's roaring title song, some excellent work from Mads Mikkelsen and Eva Green as Le Chiffre and Vesper Lynd... Everything works. Everything, except...

Cons: The Omega product placement in the train scene is howlingly poor. Aisde from that, no further notes.

Key moment: "Shaken or stirred?" "Do I look like I give a damn?"

1. From Russia With Love (1963)

In a nutshell: No matter how underrated The Living Daylights is; regardless of how iconic Goldfinger remains; despite Casino Royale being the modern benchmark to clear when it comes to Bond films... The best 007 movie is From Russia With Love. Based on Ian Fleming's best novel, it sees SPECTRE plan to avenge Bond's killing of Dr. No by luring him into a trap, using the prospect of a coveted decoder as bait. Those horrible bastards also attempt to blackmail Bond for an affair with a Soviet agent...

Pros: Terence Young's steady hand as director; Sean Connery settling into the role for his sophomore film and coming off suaver than ever; strong Hitchcockian vibes and a slow-burn suspense throughout; supporting players Robert Shaw, Pedro Armendaríz, Daniela Bianchi and Lotte Lenya are all great; a real sense of peril within one of the strongest Cold War movies ever made.

Cons: Not a single note.

Key moment: The moment before that claustrophobic train fight, when Bond's suspicions regarding Red Grant (Shaw) are confirmed because the undercover SPECTRE agent orders red wine with his fish instead of white. Is it daft? Affirmative. Snobbish? Indubitably. Does it work? Hell yes.

There we have it.

The 26th Bond film is in development, with Oscar-nominated Canadian filmmaker Denis Villeneuve directing and Steven Knight on script duties.

Production is expected to start next year, but Robert Pattinson will have to complete filming The Batman Part II (yes, he also Batman!) – production on which was temporarily paused after director Matt Reeves was faced with a personal issue. Steven Soderbergh has stepped in to help shoot the final few weeks.

This means that the earliest audiences will get to see the next Bond adventure will be in the second half of 2028 - making it seven years since No Time To Die, and the longest gap between Bond films since 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

A ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is wreaking havoc across the world - but when will we see the weather phenomenon peak – and when will it come to an end?

This impacts of this year's 'super' El Niño is expected to extend into 2027, as countries across the world continue to grapple with bouts of extreme weather.

Fiji and Bolivia have already declared a national state of disaster as drought linked to the weather phenomenon triggers widespread water shortages and devastates crops – while storms and flash floods have ravaged parts of the US.

El Niño can also weaken the polar vortex, which has already flipped and triggered a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event – sparking fears of a cold winter ahead for Europe.

How long does an El Niño last?

Typical El Niño events usually last around nine to 12 months but can go on for up to 18 months. They tend to occur every two to seven years.

Most forecasts say that this year's El Niño is forecast to peak in December, but its impacts will continue into 2027.

“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” warns WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 per cent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”

The almost-certain figure isn’t from one climate model. The WMO has coordinated ocean buoy, satellite and radiosonde data from 13 national and international centres to make the prediction.

El Niño isn’t expected to end until spring 2027, but its impacts will likely stretch further. It’s why experts warn that next year could become the hottest on record.

Is El Niño getting stronger – and what are the impacts?

On 12 October, Copernicus Climate Change Service announced that September's average sea-surface temperature reached 21.05°C – the highest on record for the month – amid strengthening El Niño conditions.

According to the WMO, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are also forecast to reach record levels during October, November and December.

Sea-surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of El Niño, are measured by the widely used Niño 3.4 index. This increased markedly from an average +1.6 °C above normal in June 2026 to +2.5 °C above normal in August. 

For October-November-December, the seasonal average Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly is forecast to reach approximately +3.7°C. This would be the highest since observations began and is stronger than the previous record of +2.6°C in November 2015-January 2016.

El Niño clashes with climate change

Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.

Human-caused global warming from the burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. It is this that paved the way for Europe’s scorching summer, long-standing drought and deadly wildfires.

Nowadays, El Niño’s impacts are compounded by an already warming world – one that has a much stronger influence on the extreme weather we’re witnessing. 2025, for example, was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally-forming cool drag of El Niño’s counterpart, La Niña.

Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño events too, by making them 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era.

“El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok in October.

“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”
